bandReport.notes:
PASSAGE MAP. My band spans parts of three 'Directions' blocks. (1) A block that OPENED ON PAGE 8 (previous band's territory): its Passage-2 begins at the foot of p08-c2 and its final sentence ('...promotion of content that generates more user engagement, regardless of how inflammatory the content may be.') is the first thing printed on p10-c1. I opened p08-c2 to read that passage in full; it governs items 13 and 14, which are the last two items of that block. Items 11-12 of that block belong to the previous band. (2) p12-c1 opens a NEW block, 'Directions for the following 3 (three) items', containing two passages: Passage-1 (schooling/class 8, on p12-c1) governs items 21 and 22; Passage-2 (science and social responsibility) begins at the foot of p12-c2, completes at the top of p14-c1, and governs item 23 ONLY. (3) p16-c1 opens a NEW block, 'Directions for the following 4 (four) items': Passage-1 (history of science, on p16-c1) governs items 31 and 32; Passage-2 (the merchant/travel, on p16-c2) governs item 33 and, per the block's 4-item count, ALSO ITEM 34 — item 34 is not printed on any of my pages, it starts on page 18 (next band's territory), and that band will need this same Passage-2 as item 34's context. Page 16 ends cleanly after item 33's four options, so lastComplete is true. Each passage is copied byte-identically across the items it governs.

COLUMN CROPS - CHECKED, NONE SLICED. The left margin of p14-c2 and p16-c2 shows a vertical ladder of stray letter fragments ('er', 'al', 'nt', 'ill', ...). This looks like a slicing defect but is the opposite: I measured the gutter and the crop boundaries on all four pages and every c2 crop STARTS LEFT OF THE GUTTER (c2 begins at x=753/750/754/733 while the left column's text ends at x=805/798/811/756), so c2 carries a redundant sliver of the left column's right edge. Every c1 crop extends past its column's last ink (c1 right edge 820/817/821/800 vs text end 805/798/811/756), so no left-column text is lost on any of my pages and I did not need to fall back to pNN.png. On p16 the footer page number straddles the two crops (c1 shows a truncated '1', c2 shows '17') — footer only, no body text affected.

TYPOGRAPHY. This paper prints NO space before a question mark ('above passage?'), unlike the 2025 paper, but DOES print a space before a colon ('have been made :'); both are transcribed as printed. Decimal points in items 26 and 27 are printed as a raised middle dot and are preserved as U+00B7 (48·75%, 93·75%, etc.). Curly quotes/apostrophes are preserved as printed (one’s, today’s, men’s, ‘graduates’, and the double-quoted epigram in Passage-1 of the p16 block and the quoted speech in item 29).

JUDGEMENT CALL - item 22 option (a). The words 'school-' and 'children.' fall on separate lines and I have transcribed them as the hyphenated compound 'school-children'. This typesetter justifies exclusively by stretching inter-word spaces and does not hyphenate words across line breaks anywhere else in the booklet, so the hyphen is read as intrinsic to the word rather than a line-break artefact. Worth a second eye against the printed page if it ever matters.

NO DEFECTS FOUND otherwise: every item in 13-33 has exactly four distinct printed options, no duplicated option text, and the numbering runs consecutively with no skips. Item 24's sequence is transcribed verbatim from a magnified crop as 'A _ BCD _ BBCDABC _ DABC _ D' (four blanks, matching the four-letter options).

questions.context: Not every voice on the internet commands the same kind of audience. When anonymous private entities with high capital can pay for more space for their opinions, they are effectively buying a louder voice. If political discourse in the digital sphere is a matter of outshining one’s opponent till the election is won, then the quality of politics suffers. The focus of social media is restricted to the promotion of content that generates more user engagement, regardless of how inflammatory the content may be.

options.label: C
options.text: Social media have been created to strengthen democracies.

options.label: D
options.text: In today’s world, social media are inevitable for well-informed social life.

questions.context: By the time children reach class 8, the bulk of them tend to be in the age range of 13 years to 15 years. But in our country, about a quarter of all children in class 8 struggle with reading simple texts and more than half are still unable to do basic arithmetic operations like division. Every year about 25 million young boys and girls from elementary school move into the life that lies for them beyond compulsory schooling. They cannot enter the workforce at least in the organized sector till they are 18. For many families, these children are the first from their families ever to get this far in school. Parents and children expect that such ‘graduates’ from school will go on to high school and college. Hardly anyone wants to go back to agriculture. On the other hand, abilities in terms of academic competencies are far lower than they should be even based on curricular expectations of class 8.

2. School curriculum that conforms to today’s requirements and is uniform for the entire country may address the issues brought out.
Which of the assumptions given above is/are valid?

questions.context: We take it for granted now that science has a social responsibility. The idea would not have occurred to Newton or Galileo. They thought of science as an account of the world as it is, and the only responsibility that they acknowledged was to tell the truth. The idea that science is a social enterprise is modern, and it begins at the industrial revolution. We are surprised that we cannot trace a social sense further back, because we nurse the illusion that the industrial revolution ended a golden age.

questions.context: “The history of science is the real history of mankind.” In this striking epigram, a nineteenth-century writer links science with its background. Like most epigrams, its power lies in emphasizing by contrast an aspect of truth which may be easily overlooked. In this case, it is easy to overlook the relations between science and mankind, and to treat the former as some abstract third party, which can sometimes be praised for its beneficial influences, but frequently and conveniently blamed for the horrors of war. Science and mankind cannot be divorced from time to time at men’s convenience. Yet we have seen that, in spite of countless opportunities of improvement, the opening years of the present period of civilization have been dominated by international conflict. Is this the inevitable result of the progress of science or does the fault lie elsewhere?
